performers: Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux, Maurice Ravel
intro: Ravel conducts the Lamoureux orchestra in Boléro, in a recording made in 1930. The snare drum plays the same rhythm throughout while a series of solo instruments take the melody in turn.

sections.label: A · Drum, plucked strings and flute
sections.mNote: The first tune begins over C and G.

sections.label: B · Solo winds over the drum
sections.mNote: The two tunes pass between solo instruments in turn.

sections.label: C · Reed choir, trombone, woodwinds
sections.mNote: Oboes and clarinets, solo trombone, then woodwinds with first violins.

sections.label: D · Both violin sections join the tune
sections.mNote: First and second violins, each divided, play with the woodwinds.

sections.label: E · The turn into E major
sections.mNote: The bass leaves its C major pattern.

sections.label: F · Trombone slides and final chord
sections.mNote: The full orchestra returns to C major.

cues.title: Snare drum, pizzicato strings, flute
cues.text: A snare drum plays a two-bar rhythm, pianissimo, that continues through the piece. Violas and cellos play pizzicato from the first bar, the cellos on C and G. The first flute enters in bar 5 with the first melody, in C major.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), printed p. 1: tempo di Bolero, moderato assai; the first snare drum, violas and cellos (pizz., pp) from bar 1; the first flute, ‘1° Solo’, pp, in bar 5. Nicolas Sceaux’s CC0 engraving of the score (https://github.com/nsceaux/Ravel_Bolero) gives the same cello and flute parts. Peter Laki’s programme note for The Cleveland Orchestra says the snare drums play the rhythm without interruption from the first bar to the last: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Polydor recording, Bal Bullier, 1930
cues.text: Ravel’s Polydor session took place at the Bal Bullier, a Paris dance hall. Albert Wolff had prepared the Lamoureux players, and Ravel conducted. Wolff conducted the other piece recorded that day, Ravel’s orchestration of his Menuet antique.
cues.evidence: Manuel Cornejo’s Maurice Ravel chronology (1930): the second recording of Boléro, at the Bal Bullier, with the Lamoureux orchestra prepared by Albert Wolff and conducted by the composer, and the first recording of Menuet antique conducted by Wolff in the same session: https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf. Phonobase entry 6574 also records that Wolff prepared the orchestra: https://phonobase.org/en/fiche/6574

cues.title: Fandango, later Boléro, 1928
cues.text: On 13 July 1928 Ravel hurried back to Paris after Joaquín Nin told him that Albéniz’s Iberia could not be orchestrated. He then worked on a piece of his own. Its working title was Fandango, and the definitive title became Boléro.
cues.evidence: Manuel Cornejo’s Maurice Ravel chronology (1928), 13 July: hurried return to Paris because Albéniz’s Iberia could not be orchestrated (information from Joaquín Nin), and work on Fandango, whose definitive title becomes Boléro: https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf. The original title Fandango and the ballet for Ida Rubinstein’s company: Peter Laki’s programme note, adapted for The Cleveland Orchestra: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero

cues.title: Ravel and Samazeuilh, Saint-Jean-de-Luz
cues.text: At Saint-Jean-de-Luz, Ravel played the theme with one finger for his friend Gustave Samazeuilh and asked whether it had “an insistent quality”. He meant to repeat it “a number of times without any development”, gradually increasing the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Gustave Samazeuilh’s recollection, quoted in Arbie Orenstein, Ravel: Man and Musician (1991), p. 98, and in A Ravel Reader (1990; 2003): “I’m going to try and repeat it a number of times without any development, gradually increasing the orchestra” (full-text excerpts seen; the “insistent quality” sentence and the page numbers were not checked in the books).

cues.title: Coppola’s recording of Boléro
cues.text: Ravel sat beside Piero Coppola at the conductor’s own recording of Boléro. Near the end Coppola increased the tempo by a fraction. Ravel jumped up and pulled at his jacket (“not so fast”), and the orchestra began again.
cues.evidence: Piero Coppola, Dix-sept ans de musique à Paris (1944), pp. 105–108, quoted in translation in Arbie Orenstein, A Ravel Reader (1990; 2003), p. 540 (full-text excerpt seen: “increased the tempo by a fraction. Ravel jumped up, came over and pulled …”). Cornejo’s chronology confirms that Ravel attended the session: https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf

cues.title: Ravel’s Polydor recording, 1930
cues.text: Ravel conducted the Lamoureux players for Polydor in January 1930. The performance filled four sides of two 78 rpm discs, so the crescendo is broken off three times before the final chord.
cues.evidence: Manuel Cornejo’s chronology (1930): the second recording of Boléro, for Polydor, made between 13 and 28 January: https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf. The BnF catalogue identifies Ravel, the orchestra, two discs and four matrices: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb38509551s.

cues.title: Oboe d’amore solo
cues.text: After flute, clarinet, bassoon and E♭ clarinet, an oboe d’amore takes the tune. It is a double reed pitched between the oboe and the cor anglais. A flute and a muted trumpet share the next statement.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), p. 11: oboe d’amore melody before rehearsal 5, where trumpet and flute enter. Gurminder K. Bhogal, Music Theory Online 26.2 (2020), ¶3.4, places the oboe d’amore at rehearsal 4 and the flute with muted trumpet at rehearsal 5: https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.2/mto.20.26.2.bhogal.html. Peter Laki’s programme note for The Cleveland Orchestra lists the order of solo instruments and describes the oboe d’amore: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute and muted trumpet, rehearsal 5
cues.text: At rehearsal 5 a flute and a muted trumpet play the tune an octave apart, the trumpet mp and the flute pp. It is the first time in the piece that two instruments share the melody. Jennifer Beavers described the pair as fused into one stream.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), p. 11, rehearsal 5: trumpet con sord. marked 1° Solo, mp, and flute in octaves, pp. Jennifer Beavers, Music Theory Online 25.4 (2019), paragraph 6.2, describes the flute and muted trumpet as an exception among the opening solos, fused into one stream: https://www.mtosmt.org/issues/mto.19.25.4/mto.19.25.4.beavers.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Saxophones on Ravel’s Polydor recording
cues.text: The tenor saxophone takes the tune first, then the higher saxophones. On Ravel’s Polydor record Priam plays the tenor part and Marcel Mule the soprano.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), pp. 14–18: tenor saxophone solo at rehearsal 6, then the sopranino and soprano saxophone parts. Phonobase entry 6574 names M. Mule on soprano saxophone and M. Priam on tenor in the Polydor recording (matrices 566030–31): https://phonobase.org/en/fiche/6574

cues.title: Horn, celesta and two piccolos
cues.text: Two piccolos, a celesta and a solo horn play the tune together. The horn is in C, the celesta two and three octaves above, and the piccolos in G and E. The four parts are spaced like the overtones of the horn’s note, and Jennifer Beavers likens their combined sound to an organ stop.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), printed p. 22: horn, celesta and two piccolos carrying the melody after rehearsal 8, with the piccolo staves signed for G and E. Jennifer Beavers, Music Theory Online 25.4 (2019), paragraphs 4.2 and 6.2: horn, celesta and piccolos, spaced as the harmonic series, fuse into a single stream that “evokes the sound of an organ stop”: https://www.mtosmt.org/issues/mto.19.25.4/mto.19.25.4.beavers.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tenth statement, oboes and clarinets
cues.text: Oboe, oboe d’amore, cor anglais and clarinets play the tenth statement of the melody together, each marked mf. The ninth statement is for horn, celesta and two piccolos. The eleventh is for a solo trombone.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), printed pp. 22–23: horn, celesta and two piccolos before rehearsal 9; oboe, oboe d’amore, cor anglais and clarinets, each marked mf, from two bars after rehearsal 9. Statements are counted from the first flute entry in bar 5 and run eighteen bars each, so the statement two bars after rehearsal 8 is the ninth. Gurminder K. Bhogal, Music Theory Online 26.2 (2020), ¶¶3.5–3.6, has the doubling ‘across five levels’ at rehearsal 9 and the trombone at rehearsal 10: https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.2/mto.20.26.2.bhogal.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Death of Jacques Durand, 1928
cues.text: On 23 August 1928 Ravel broke off the orchestration of Boléro to travel to Avon, where his publisher Jacques Durand had died the day before. He finished the piece on 15 October. The next day he signed a contract with Durand’s firm for its sale, for 20,000 francs.
cues.evidence: Cornejo’s chronology (1928): 22 August, death of Jacques Durand; 23 August, Ravel interrupts the orchestration of Bolero to travel to Avon; 15 October, finishes composition; 16 October, contract with Durand for 20,000 francs: https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf

cues.title: Ravel on Boléro, 1931
cues.text: Ravel called Boléro “orchestral tissue without music”, a seventeen-minute piece built as one long crescendo. He told Joaquín Nin it had “no form, properly speaking, no development, no or almost no modulation”. In 1931 he added that it contained practically no invention except the plan.
cues.evidence: Ravel to Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi, The Daily Telegraph, 11 July 1931 (“a piece lasting seventeen minutes and consisting wholly of ‘orchestral tissue without music’ … practically no invention except the plan”), as quoted in Roger Nichols, Ravel (2011), in The Cambridge Companion to Ravel (2000) and in Orenstein, A Ravel Reader (2003), p. 477. Ravel to Joaquín Nin, La Revue musicale (1938), p. 213 (“no form properly speaking, no development, no or almost no modulation”), as quoted in Deborah Mawer, The Ballets of Maurice Ravel (2006), p. 219, and in Nichols (full-text excerpts seen).

cues.title: Violins in the melody
cues.text: In the fourteenth statement both violin sections play the melody, each divided in two, with the woodwinds and tenor saxophone. The first violins had joined it in the thirteenth, with flutes, oboes and clarinets.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), printed pp. 37 and 41: first violins, marked arco, in the melody with flutes, piccolo, oboes and clarinets from two bars after rehearsal 12; first and second violins, marked Div. and arco, in the melody from two bars after rehearsal 13. Statements are counted from the first flute entry in bar 5 and run eighteen bars each. Nicolas Sceaux’s CC0 engraving (https://github.com/nsceaux/Ravel_Bolero, first and second violin parts) has the same entries. Peter Laki’s programme note for The Cleveland Orchestra names the strings last among the instruments that take the tune: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ballet première, Paris Opéra, 1928
cues.text: The Paris Opéra gave Boléro as a ballet on 22 November 1928, with choreography by Bronislava Nijinska and sets by Alexandre Benois, and a woman dancing on a tavern table. Diaghilev, Stravinsky and the princesse de Polignac attended. Ravel was on tour in Spain.
cues.evidence: Cornejo’s chronology (22 November 1928): première of the ballet at the Opéra de Paris, choreography by Nijinska, sets by Benois, attended by Diaghilev, Misia, the princesse de Polignac and Stravinsky; Ravel was not there (he was in Madrid on 22–23 November): https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf. The scenario, a Spanish tavern with a woman stamping out the rhythm on a table: Peter Laki’s programme note, adapted for The Cleveland Orchestra, which quotes a summary by an unnamed writer: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero

cues.title: Interview, Evening Standard, 1932
cues.text: In 1932 Ravel told the London Evening Standard: “It was a factory which inspired my Boléro. I would like it always to be played with a vast factory in the background.”
cues.evidence: The 1932 London Evening Standard interview, as quoted in Peter Laki’s programme note, adapted for The Cleveland Orchestra: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero (the interview itself was not opened).

cues.title: Toscanini’s tempo, Paris Opéra, 1930
cues.text: On 4 May 1930 Toscanini conducted Boléro at the Paris Opéra, faster than Ravel liked. In one report, Ravel said backstage “That’s not my tempo”, and Toscanini replied that at Ravel’s tempo it was not effective. Ravel answered, “Then do not play it.”
cues.evidence: Cornejo’s chronology, 4 May 1930: Toscanini conducts Bolero at the New York Philharmonic’s festival at the Opéra de Paris, attended by the composer, vexed: https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf. The exchange (“That’s not my tempo”; “When I play your tempo …”) appears in John Rink, ed., Musical Performance: A Guide to Understanding (Cambridge, 2002) (full-text excerpt seen); the closing line is reported in Dunoyer (1993), p. 97 (not opened).

cues.title: E major at rehearsal 18
cues.text: At rehearsal 18 the key moves from C to E major for eight bars. The first melody returns, fortissimo, and the bass plays E and B. The snare drum rhythm continues.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), printed pp. 63–65: rehearsal 18 and the eight bars in E major that end where bass drum, cymbals and tam-tam enter. In Nicolas Sceaux’s CC0 engraving (https://github.com/nsceaux/Ravel_Bolero) the basses play E and B and the timpani E in these bars. Gurminder K. Bhogal, Music Theory Online 26.2 (2020), ¶¶3.8–3.10: the shift to E major at rehearsal 18, with the first melody in new fortissimo scoring: https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.2/mto.20.26.2.bhogal.html. Jennifer Beavers, Music Theory Online 25.4 (2019), ¶6.2, also names the motion to E major at rehearsal 18.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last six bars
cues.text: Six bars from the end the bass drum, cymbals and tam-tam play for the first time, and the trombones and saxophones play glissandos. The harmony returns to C, and the final chord is C major.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), printed pp. 65–66: bass drum, cymbals and tam-tam enter six bars from the end, with glissando marks for the trombones. In Nicolas Sceaux’s CC0 engraving (https://github.com/nsceaux/Ravel_Bolero) the percussion parts begin in bar 335 and the cellos end on C–G–E–C. Gurminder K. Bhogal, Music Theory Online 26.2 (2020), ¶¶3.7 and 3.11: glissandi of trombones and saxophones ‘six measures from the end’, with gong and tam-tam: https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.2/mto.20.26.2.bhogal.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
